generatedProse.concept-context: In any subject, searching for sources is rarely a quick lookup. When you look for evidence on a question, you are exploring something the field is still working out, not fetching a single fact. You try some terms, see what comes back, and search again with better ones. Treating a search as exploratory, iterative and planned is what academic searching asks of you, whatever you study.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students given the same question and told to find sources for it.

{{learner-a}} types the whole question into a search box, glances at the first few results, and picks the one at the top. The search is over in a minute. But {{learner-a}} has treated this like looking up a fact: one attempt, no plan, and whatever came first. There was no sense of what a good source would look like, or how to look again. This is everyday searching.

{{learner-b}} starts by asking what the question is really about and what sort of evidence would answer it. She tries a few terms, sees what comes back, and searches again with better words when the first set is too broad. Her search takes longer, but it is exploratory, iterative and planned. This is academic searching.

Both students searched. Only {{learner-b}} treated searching as a discipline rather than a quick lookup.
generatedProse.summary: Academic searching is more than looking something up. It is exploratory, because you are following a question your field is still working out; iterative, because you search again with better words; and strategy-driven, because you plan before you start. You can now explain what academic searching is and tell it apart from the everyday searching you already do. The next lesson looks at what makes a search effective.

check.body: In the worked example, what made {{learner-b}}'s approach academic rather than everyday?

items.text: She planned what she wanted, tried some terms, and searched again with better ones.
She finished the search more quickly than {{learner-a}} did.
She typed the whole question into the search box.
She picked the result at the top of the list.

feedback.correct: That's right. Planning, trying terms and searching again is academic searching in action.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what {{learner-b}} DID differently, beyond finishing fast or taking the first result.
feedback.incorrectFinal: {{learner-b}} was academic because she planned, tried terms and searched again. Finishing fast, typing the whole question or taking the top result are all the everyday approach.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; carry the cast only through the {{learner-a}} (weaker) and {{learner-b}} (stronger) tokens, never a literal name (the pack supplies the whole body, but not the names). Each example paragraph must begin with its token, weaker first - merge-context.js's wrapProse() only emits the we-weaker/we-stronger cue classes for a paragraph that leads with the token. The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
